request.report:
Completed A/greedy (ngram-mod defaults) and analyzed both off and A. Full results in bench/results/2026-10-12/m1-ngram/replay/{off,A}-greedy/, written up in bench/m1-notes.md §9.

Findings (decode tok/s = sum(predicted_n)/sum(predicted_ms), per phase; fresh server per phase; same max_tokens per request in both arms):
- single-agent: off 55.1 -> A 86.0 tok/s
- single-mem: off 55.6 -> A 53.1 (slower)
- dual-agent fg: off 26.3 -> A 25.5 (slower); combined off 25.6 -> A 26.1 (marginal, not a win)
- dual-mem fg: off 25.0 -> A 23.8 (slower); combined off 26.1 -> A 25.0 (slower)

Draft acceptance (A): single-agent 75.5% (6212/8229), single/dual-mem 9.32% (69/740), dual-agent fg 13.95% (259/1856).

Temperature-0 output identity (off vs A, per phase): single-agent 3/30 same, single-mem 10/12 same, dual-agent 10/38 same, dual-mem 11/19 same. The single-agent "speedup" is an artifact: A generated +30% more tokens (14044 vs 10813) and added 2 more length finishes, and even same-prompt rows differ (e.g. r0/0/2: same prompt_n/cache_n/length, different sha). So ngram-mod is not a deterministic drop-in speedup.

VRAM identical for off and A after first fg request: 9507 MiB (vram.txt). mmproj + ngram works, no -nommproj fallback needed: draft-acceptance lines present in A server_*.log, no 'not supported by this context'/'unsupported batch.has_embd'.

Decision so far: do NOT deploy — ngram-mod does not help when both slots are busy (it is slower in every dual phase) and perturbs greedy outputs.

Wrote §9 (results), §10 (Config B = ngram-simple, justified: distinct ngram family, same ~48-token draft budget, lets me confirm the no-deployment decision is robust to variant), §11 (next steps). Next: run B/greedy, then prod for off and whichever of A/B has higher dual-agent tok/s.
request.why: Config B (ngram-simple defaults) greedy replay, 4 phases on fresh servers at :8089. Completes the >=2 ngram-setting sweep before the prod runs; justifies the no-deployment decision on robustness to ngram variant.
